883.title: the crossing of the Yamuna
883.hook: on the far bank, a whole village is asleep, and Vasudeva has to leave his son beside a sleeping stranger
883.howItsDone: Hindus honor Yashoda as Krishna's foster mother, and Nanda's household in Gokula is remembered in songs and festivals of Krishna's childhood; Nandotsava, the celebration in Nanda's village, is kept by some communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the crossing of the Yamuna began: the guards asleep, the doors open, Shesha's hoods over the father and child, the river making way. Who did you thank for holding off the rain? Day eight hundred eighty-three.

Gokula is silent. Vasudeva has come up out of the river, soaked, with the baby in his arms, and he walks into the cowherd village where his friend Nanda lives. Nobody stops him. Nobody even stirs. The Bhagavata says he found everyone in Nanda's household fast asleep. Inside, Nanda's wife Yashoda has just given birth too. She is lying beside a newborn girl, so deeply asleep that she doesn't know what kind of child she has had. Today, what he does in that room.
screen: `GOKULA IS SILENT.` → `NANDA'S HOUSE ASLEEP.` → `YASHODA AND A NEWBORN GIRL.`

segments.voice: He makes the exchange. He lays his son down beside Yashoda. He picks up her daughter. And he walks back the way he came, back across the river, back through the open doors, back into the prison. He sets the girl down on Devaki's bed. The text says he put the fetters back on his own feet, and the doors closed, as if nothing had happened. Sit with that for a second. This is the man who walked out into a flood to save his son, and the end of his journey is to give that son away, to a woman who doesn't know, in a house where he cannot stay, and then walk himself back into chains. The rescue only works if he goes back. And there is the girl. She is someone else's newborn daughter, and he is carrying her into the prison where Kamsa killed Devaki's children. The Bhagavata has told us who she is: Yogamaya, the Lord's own power, born to Yashoda for exactly this. Vasudeva may not fully know. He carries her anyway. And Yashoda. She will wake up to a son. In the stories ahead she is his mother in every way they show: the one who feeds him, chases him, scolds him, and ties him up when he steals butter. A crossing usually means getting to the other side and staying there. This one means leaving the most precious thing on the other side, and coming home with empty arms.
screen: `THE EXCHANGE IN THE DARK` · `BACK ACROSS, BACK INTO CHAINS` · `THE GIRL IS YOGAMAYA` · then, large: `YASHODA WAKES UP A MOTHER`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let your arms rest. Bring to mind someone you have had to entrust to other people: a child at school, a parent in someone's care, a friend going far away, a project you handed over. Breathe in, and see them safe on the other side. Breathe out, and let your hands open, a little. You can care deeply and still let someone else hold them. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The crossing of the Yamuna. Vasudeva leaves his son with Yashoda, carries her daughter back, and returns to his chains.

segments.voice: Your line: the crossing of the Yamuna. Today, let someone else carry something you love, and trust them with it. Day eight hundred eighty-three.

884.title: the crossing of the Yamuna
884.hook: a baby cries in the prison, Kamsa comes running, and the child he reaches for slips out of his hands into the sky
884.howItsDone: Hindus who follow the Bhagavata honor the girl born to Yashoda as Yogamaya, a form of the Goddess, and in some places she is worshiped as a sister of Krishna.

segments.voice: Yesterday the crossing of the Yamuna ended in Nanda's house: Vasudeva left his son by sleeping Yashoda and carried her daughter back into the prison. Whom did you trust with something you love? Day eight hundred eighty-four.

A newborn cries in the cell. The guards jerk awake and run to tell the king. Kamsa leaps out of bed, the Bhagavata says, his hair loose, stumbling, and rushes to the prison. This is the eighth child. This is the one the voice warned him about at the wedding. Devaki holds the baby close and begs him. It's a girl, she says, a daughter of your own house. Don't kill a girl. You've taken so many of my children. Leave me just this one. Kamsa doesn't hear her. He tears the child out of her arms. Today, what happens to the girl Vasudeva carried back.
screen: `A CRY IN THE CELL.` → `KAMSA RUNS TO THE PRISON.` → `"IT'S A GIRL. LEAVE ME THIS ONE."`

segments.voice: He swings the baby by the feet to dash her against a stone. And she slips out of his grip. She rises into the air above him, and she is no longer a baby. The Bhagavata calls her the younger sister of Vishnu. She appears as a goddess with eight arms, holding weapons, wearing garlands and bright clothes, with celestial beings singing her praise. And she speaks down to him. What will you gain by killing me, fool? The one who will kill you has already been born, somewhere else. Stop killing the helpless for nothing. Then she is gone. The text says she came to be worshiped on earth in many places, under many names. Look at the shape of it. Kamsa grabbed the one child in the story who could not be harmed, and the attempt only revealed the truth. The crossing worked. The boy is safe on the other side of the river, and now even Kamsa knows it. And then, for a moment, Kamsa breaks. He frees Devaki and Vasudeva from their chains. He apologizes. He even weeps, and says that everyone acts under fate, and that he has been cruel. Devaki and Vasudeva forgive him. It's a gentle moment, from Kamsa of all people. It doesn't last. The next morning his ministers advise him that, if the child is somewhere out there, newborns across the land should be hunted. Kamsa agrees. The goddess told him to stop killing the helpless. He hears it, and chooses fear anyway.
screen: `SHE SLIPS FROM HIS GRIP` · `THE GODDESS WITH EIGHT ARMS` · `"YOUR KILLER IS BORN ELSEWHERE"` · then, large: `KAMSA FREES THEM, THEN CHOOSES FEAR`

Breathe out, and let your grip on it loosen, even a little, the way the child slipped from Kamsa's hands. If you pray, you can offer that fear in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The crossing of the Yamuna. The boy is safe across the river, and the girl Kamsa seizes rises as a goddess to tell him so.

885.title: Putana
885.hook: a beautiful stranger walks into Nanda's house, smiling, and picks up the baby, and nobody stops her
885.howItsDone: The killing of Putana is told in the Bhagavata Purana's tenth book and is one of the childhood episodes Hindus retell in songs, dance-dramas and temple art about Krishna.

segments.voice: Yesterday the crossing of the Yamuna came to its end: the girl slipped from Kamsa's hands as a goddess, and Kamsa, after a moment of remorse, chose fear and sent his people after newborns. Did you loosen your grip on anything? Day eight hundred eighty-five.

Nanda is away. He has gone to Mathura to pay his dues to the king, and Vasudeva, meeting him there, has warned him: go home quickly, there may be trouble in Gokula. Back in the village, a woman arrives. She is beautiful, the Bhagavata says, with flowers in her hair, a soft smile, a graceful walk. The cowherd women see her and think a goddess has come to visit. She walks straight into Nanda's house, to the bed where the baby is lying. Her name is today's word.
screen: `NANDA IS AWAY.` → `A BEAUTIFUL STRANGER.` → `SHE WALKS TO THE BABY'S BED.`

segments.voice: Putana is one of the killers Kamsa has sent out. The Bhagavata calls her a demoness who goes from town to town killing infants, who can travel through the air and take whatever shape she likes. Today she has taken the shape of a lovely woman. And here is the first unsettling detail. Yashoda and Rohini are right there. They see her lift the child. They are so struck by her beauty and her sweetness that they just stand and watch. The danger doesn't break in. It is welcomed. And the text turns the picture around: Putana takes the child on her lap the way someone picks up a sleeping snake, thinking it is a rope. The danger she doesn't see is the baby. And the child? The Bhagavata says that when she came near, he closed his eyes. The verse doesn't say why. Commentators have offered more than one reason: that he was hiding his power, perhaps, or turning from her cruelty. Putana takes him on her lap and offers him her breast, which she has smeared with poison. And the baby feeds. But he takes more than milk. He draws her very life out with it. She begins to scream: let go, let go. She thrashes, sweating, her eyes rolling. The earth shakes at her cry. And as she dies, her disguise falls away. She collapses in her true form, so enormous that, the text says, trees are crushed beneath her. On top of that terrible body, the cowherd women find the baby, playing, unafraid. Danger came with a smile and was welcomed in. The child knew. And the one who came to feed him poison is undone by the act of feeding.
screen: `A KILLER IN A LOVELY FORM` · `THE MOTHERS JUST WATCH` · `HE CLOSES HIS EYES` · then, large: `"LET GO, LET GO"`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let your eyes close if you like, the way the child's did. Breathe out, and simply see it for what it is. Seeing clearly is enough for this sit. If you pray, you can ask in your own way for clear sight. The bell holds the time.

886.title: Putana
886.hook: the cowherds burn Putana's body, and the smoke that rises smells sweet, like fragrant wood
886.howItsDone: Vaishnava teachers and devotees retell Putana's story as an example of Krishna's grace, and the protective rites the cowherd women perform are described in the Bhagavata alongside the names of Vishnu they recite.

segments.voice: Yesterday Putana came smiling into Nanda's house with poison, and the baby drew her life out as he fed. What came to you smiling yesterday, and did you let it in? Day eight hundred eighty-six.

The cowherd women snatch the baby up off Putana's body and carry him away, shaking. Then they protect him the way they know how. The Bhagavata describes it closely: they wave a cow's tail around him, wash him, mark his body with the dust of cows, and touch his limbs one by one while saying names of Vishnu, asking each name to guard a part of him. Feet. Knees. Belly. Heart. Then Yashoda nurses him and puts him to sleep. The danger is over. What the story does next with Putana is the surprise.
screen: `THE WOMEN TAKE THE BABY.` → `A NAME FOR EVERY LIMB.` → `YASHODA NURSES HIM TO SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Nanda comes home from Mathura with the other cowherds and finds a giant body lying across the village. He remembers Vasudeva's warning and is amazed: the man saw it coming. The cowherds cut up the body, pile it on a fire and burn it. And the smoke smells sweet. The Bhagavata says it rose fragrant, like aloe wood. Why would the pyre of a child-killer smell like incense? The text gives its own answer. Because the child had drunk her milk, her wrongs were burned away. And then the narrator, the sage Shuka, says something astonishing. Putana came to kill. She smeared poison on her breast and offered it to the Lord. Even so, because she offered him milk, she reached the place given to a mother. If even she, who came with murder in mind, was given that, Shuka asks, what of those who offer him love? That is the hinge of this story. The Bhagavata doesn't dwell on punishing her. It dwells on the one thing she did that looked like a mother's act, and treats it as hers. Some Vaishnava teachers read this as a picture of grace: the Lord responds to the offering itself, and his touch transforms even an offering made in bad faith. Notice the order. First the village protects its child with every name it knows. Then the enemy's smoke rises sweet. The same story holds both: the right to guard what you love, and a mercy wider than anyone in the village expected.
screen: `NANDA REMEMBERS THE WARNING` · `THE SMOKE RISES SWEET` · `SHUKA: SHE REACHED A MOTHER'S PLACE` · then, large: `A MERCY WIDER THAN EXPECTED`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath come and go. First, do what the cowherd women did, in your own way: bring to mind someone you want to protect, and hold them for a few breaths. Breathe out, and let that small thing be true too. If you pray, you can hold both people in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Putana. She came with poison, and because she offered milk, the Bhagavata says she reached a mother's place.

887.title: the butter thief
887.howItsDone: Krishna as the butter thief is a familiar figure in Hindu devotion: images of the child Krishna with butter in his hand are kept in homes and temples, and on Janmashtami some communities hang pots of curd high up for teams to climb and break.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Putana: she came to the baby with poison, and the text says even she was blessed, because she had fed him like a mother. Who has given you more than they meant to? Day eight hundred eighty-seven.

A group of women is standing at Yashoda's door, and they have a list. They are the gopis, the cowherd women of the village, and Putana is gone. Now there's a different problem, and he's a toddler. Butter has been disappearing all over the village. Curd too. Milk pots are broken. And every trail leads back to this house. So they come to his mother, half laughing, half fed up, and they make their case. Today the Bhagavata Purana lets us hear the complaint, item by item.
screen: `WOMEN AT YASHODA'S DOOR.` → `BUTTER IS DISAPPEARING.` → `EVERY TRAIL LEADS HERE.`

segments.voice: Here is their list, as the text gives it. He turns the calves loose before milking time, and when someone scolds him, he laughs. He finds a way into the milk and curd and eats it, and when he's had his fill, he feeds the rest to the monkeys. If a monkey won't eat, he breaks the pot. People hang their pots high from the ceiling on ropes, to keep them out of his reach. So he drags over stools and a mortar and climbs. Or he makes a hole in the bottom of the hanging pot and drinks from underneath. In a dark storeroom he doesn't even need a lamp: the jewels he wears light the way. That's the case for the prosecution. Then comes the turn. While they're telling all this, Krishna is sitting right there beside his mother, with wide, frightened eyes, the picture of a child who has never touched a pot in his life. The women look at that face, and they can't keep scolding. They laugh. And Yashoda, the text says, smiles and doesn't have the heart to punish him. Notice what kind of complaint this is. Nobody stops making butter. Nobody locks the door. They keep coming to his mother to report him, and in the reporting they get to talk about him, and be near him. Some devotional teachers read the stolen butter as the heart of the devotee: the thing you hang up high, out of reach, and that he finds a way into anyway. Whether you take it that way or simply as a story about a little boy, the village is full of people who keep leaving the butter out.
screen: `THE CALVES, THE MONKEYS, THE POTS.` · `STOOLS, A MORTAR, A HOLE IN THE POT.` · `THE INNOCENT FACE.` · then, large: `THEY CAN'T KEEP SCOLDING.`

segments.voice: Settle in, and let your hands rest. Bring to mind a small person you love, or the small person you once were, caught in some harmless mischief. A face covered in something sticky. If there is a warmer one, breathe with it. If you pray, you can say Krishna's name, or a name for God you already use, once, quietly. The bell holds the time.
The butter thief. Krishna as a toddler, raiding the village's pots, and the village that can't stay angry at him.

888.title: the butter thief
888.howItsDone: Krishna bound by Yashoda's rope is remembered in his name Damodara, and some Vaishnava communities honor this story in the autumn month of Kartika with songs and lamps offered to Damodara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the butter thief: the gopis brought Yashoda their list, and one look at his frightened face stopped the scolding. Did you smile before you corrected someone? Day eight hundred eighty-eight.

Early morning in Nanda's house. The servants are busy elsewhere, and Yashoda is churning curd herself. She pulls the rope back and forth around the churning stick, her bangles moving with her arms, and as she works, the text says, she sings about the things her little boy has done. Then the little boy arrives. He's hungry, he wants his mother, and he takes hold of the churning stick so she can't go on. She stops, lifts him into her lap, and feeds him. It's a perfectly quiet scene. It's about to fall apart.
screen: `YASHODA CHURNING, SINGING.` → `HE GRABS THE CHURNING STICK.` → `A QUIET MORNING.`

segments.voice: On the fire, the milk starts to boil over. Yashoda sets Krishna down, mid-meal, and runs to it. He's furious. He bites his lip, picks up a stone, and cracks open the pot of curd. Then he slips into another room and starts eating butter in secret. Yashoda comes back to a broken pot and no child. She follows the trail and finds him standing on an upturned mortar, handing butter from the hanging pot to a monkey, glancing around in case anyone sees. So she picks up a stick. He sees her, jumps down, and runs, and she runs after him. The Bhagavata pauses here to marvel: the one the yogis can't reach even with their minds is being chased around the yard by his mother. She catches him. He cries and rubs his eyes, smearing them. She drops the stick, and decides instead to tie him to the mortar, so he'll stay put. She takes a rope and ties it around his waist. It's too short, by just two fingers' width. She adds another rope. Still two fingers short. She brings every rope in the house, and it's always two fingers short, and the neighbor women start laughing, and so does she. By now she's sweating, and the flowers are slipping from her hair. Krishna sees how tired his mother is. And then, the text says, he lets himself be tied. That's the heart of it. Nothing in the universe can hold him. A tired mother's love can, because he allows it. Tradition says this is where one of his names comes from, Damodara, the one with a rope around his waist.
screen: `THE MILK BOILS OVER.` · `A BROKEN POT, A MONKEY, A STICK.` · `ALWAYS TWO FINGERS SHORT.` · then, large: `HE LETS HIMSELF BE TIED.`

Breathe out, and soften, the way Krishna softened when he saw his mother's face. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer for these breaths. The bell holds the time.
The butter thief. A child no rope could hold, letting his mother tie him once he saw how hard she was trying.
Your line: the butter thief. Today, notice one person working hard on your behalf, and let them know you see it. Day eight hundred eighty-eight.

889.title: the butter thief
889.howItsDone: The freeing of Kubera's sons, called Yamalarjuna in Sanskrit, the twin arjuna trees, is retold in Krishna devotion as part of the Damodara story, and some images show the child pulling the mortar between two trees.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the butter thief let himself be tied, once he saw how tired his mother was. Whose hard work did you notice? Day eight hundred eighty-nine.
screen: `THE BUTTER THIEF.` · `HE LETS HIMSELF BE TIED.`

segments.voice: So there he is, a small boy roped to a heavy wooden mortar, and his mother has gone back to her housework. A child might sulk, or cry. Krishna looks around the yard. Near the house stand two tall arjuna trees, side by side, close together. And the Bhagavata lets us in on something nobody in the village knows. Those two trees used to be people. They've been standing there a long time, waiting for this exact boy. Today the mortar goes for a walk.

segments.voice: The trees were once Nalakuvara and Manigriva, the sons of Kubera, the god of wealth. The text tells their story. Proud and drunk, they were playing in a river with a crowd of young women, wearing nothing, when the sage Narada happened by. The women, embarrassed, covered themselves at once. The two brothers didn't bother. So Narada cursed them to stand as trees. But his curse came with its own way out: they would stand until they saw Krishna, and then be free. A curse, in this telling, that was also a kindness, because what they lacked was humility, and a tree has time to learn it. Now Krishna crawls toward them, dragging the mortar behind him. He squeezes between the two trunks. The mortar doesn't fit. It turns sideways and wedges against them. He pulls. And with a great crack, both trees come crashing down. Out of them step two shining figures. They bow to the child, praise him, ask that their speech and eyes and hands be given to him from now on, and they leave. The cowherds come running at the noise. Who did this? The children who were playing nearby say: Krishna did, dragging the mortar. The grown-ups can hardly believe it. Nanda unties his son, smiling. Look back at this week. A baby carried across a flooding river at night. Putana, blessed in spite of herself. A village that can't stay angry at a thief. And a punishment, a boy tied to a mortar, that becomes the way two prisoners go free.

Just breathe with it, and ask quietly: is anything being freed, or learned, because I'm stuck here? Let the question rest without an answer if none comes.
